html_en:
Spain's Copa América triumph dominated the tech community's timelines, but the more durable conversations were about something bigger: how AI is quietly rewiring commerce, creativity, and the economics of software itself.

⚽ The Beautiful Game, Ugly Tactics

Half of AI Twitter spent Sunday watching football. Spain beat Argentina in what sounds like a deeply unsatisfying final. Matt Turck was unsparing:

"All the aggravation, attitude, fouls, taunting, vulgarity, fans throwing bottles at fans from the opposing team, to produce ZERO shot on goal during the final." — @mattturck

Nikunj echoed the frustration with Argentina's tactics: "Each player is so SO good. Why all the antics? Constantly complaining and looking for a foul while playing haramball the entire game." Meanwhile, Guillermo Rauch was gracious in defeat: "Thankful to 🇦🇷 Argentina for giving it all. Grit, passion, talent, faith. To Messi for proving he's the best ever. Enhorabuena tíos 🇪🇸!"

💳 Agentic Commerce Is No Longer Hypothetical

The most substantive content of the day came from the MAD Podcast, where Matt Turck sat down with Emily Sands, Head of Data and AI at Stripe. The conversation is a must-listen for anyone building in or investing around the AI application layer.

Watch/Listen: Stripe's AI Chief: How AI Agents Will Buy, Sell, and Pay — The MAD Podcast

Sands sketched out a "levels of autonomy" framework for agentic commerce — analogous to self-driving car classifications — ranging from AI-assisted checkout all the way to fully autonomous agents running business procurement. Stripe has already deployed real infrastructure: partnerships with Google (merchants selling inside AI Mode and Gemini), OpenAI and Microsoft (products discoverable in ChatGPT and Copilot), and Meta (checkout inside ads). The near-future she's building toward:

"I have a $500 budget for back to school shopping, and you already know everything about my kids and their school and where I live. So, like, get it done." — Emily Sands, Stripe

But the sleeper topic was token theft. Sands called it "the most under-discussed topic in all of AI":

"Fraudsters have figured out that in AI, you actually don't really need to steal money or credentials. You can just steal tokens. More than one in six signups at AI companies are this kind of abuse — the dine and dash, but it's for tokens." — Emily Sands, Stripe

As agents gain the ability to transact autonomously, the fraud surface grows dramatically. This is infrastructure work that most product teams aren't thinking about yet.

📉 Why Cheaper AI Means More AI Spend — And Why Open Models Change Regulation Math

Aaron Levie was in fine form, threading together several of the day's biggest macro ideas. On the counterintuitive economics of falling token prices:

"A lot of people make the mistake of thinking that when AI costs drop, that spend on AI drops with it. Usually the opposite happens. When you make AI cheaper, it will get consumed more. You start to write more code. You review more code for bugs and security. You run agents on large data sets you couldn't process before." — @levie

On why AI diffusion is faster in software than in life sciences or sales — and what that means for where the real opportunity lies:

"The reason coding has been adopted so quickly is you can write a near infinite amount of code, test it, and run it without anyone in the outside world ever having to do anything differently. This is not true for life sciences, where new drug development eventually needs to be tested for years." — @levie

And on the regulation debate, where the emergence of capable open-weights models reshapes the calculus entirely:

"In a world where there are strong open source alternatives only just behind the frontier models, you make yourself less secure and competitive by gatekeeping access to frontier model capabilities. Even if America could fully ban access to open source models, other ecosystems wouldn't have that ban — and they'd have a leg up." — @levie

On a related note, Rauch argued that cybersecurity is the real IQ test for AI models — far more demanding than cloning an app — and flagged Kimi K3's strong performance on security benchmarks as a bullish signal for open models broadly.

🛠️ The Texture of Daily AI Work

Several builders shared more granular glimpses of AI in their actual workflows. Cat Wu shared her prompt for using Claude Cowork as a calendar manager — a surprisingly rich use case:

"Manage my calendar for the week. Requirements: 1. <20 hours of meetings 2. Dedupe conflicting meetings. Look at past weeks to see what kinds of meetings I decline. Dinners don't count against the 20 hours. Build a skill that you refine. Ask me before updating invites." — @_catwu

Dan Shipper noted a quiet but meaningful inflection point at Every: "Have been able to automatically do ~70% of the copy edits we would ordinarily do by hand internally for the last week. First time that's happened and I've been trying it for years." That's not a demo — that's a workflow transformation.

Zara Zhang made a crisp observation about how AI is changing software's relationship with permanence: "We need to get used to the idea that code/software can now be disposable" — spinning up throwaway dashboards, design playgrounds, HTML explainers, all discarded after use.

And Garry Tan made a quietly sharp point about data formats in a world of rapidly evolving AI stacks: "Markdown files are universal and will survive millennia. Unsurprisingly they are a fantastic data format when the intelligence stack is in flux at this extreme pace." Durability of format matters more, not less, when everything else is moving fast.
html_zh:
从世界杯决赛的激情到AI代理商务的冷静分析，今天的科技圈在两个截然不同的话题之间切换——但真正的主角，是那个悄然重塑商业基础设施的"代理经济"。

🤖 AI代理正在学会花钱——以及被盗刷

Stripe的数据与AI负责人Emily Sense在 The MAD Podcast 中描绘了一个令人着迷的图景：AI代理正在从"帮你找鞋"演变为"帮你买鞋"，乃至"帮你管一门生意"。Stripe已与Google、Microsoft、OpenAI和Meta达成合作，让商品能够直接在Gemini、ChatGPT和Copilot等AI界面内完成购买。

"我们有一个完整的自主等级框架——就像自动驾驶的L1到L3。消费者端目前大约处于L2：人类还在主导决策，但开始把一部分选择权委托给AI。我们距离'我有500美元的开学购物预算，你知道我孩子的一切，去搞定它'的那个世界，还需要一两年。"
— Emily Sense，The MAD Podcast

但这个新世界也带来了新的安全威胁。Emily提到了一个几乎被整个行业忽视的问题：

"欺诈者已经发现，在AI领域你根本不需要偷钱或偷凭证——你只需要偷Token。当我看到数据时，规模之大让我震惊：AI公司超过六分之一的注册行为都是这类滥用。这是'Token版蹭饭跑单'。"
— Emily Sense

💸 降价不会杀死AI需求，反而会放大它

Aaron Levie 今天连发数条深度推文，提出了一个反直觉的观点：AI推理成本下降，不会压缩AI支出，而会扩大它。

"当AI变得更便宜，它会被消耗得更多。因为现在你负担得起把它用于更广泛的任务——你开始写更多代码，审查更多代码漏洞，在以前无法处理的大型数据集上跑Agent。因此，在可预见的未来，任何降低Token成本的事情都会推高推理需求。"
— @levie

他还犀利地指出了AI扩散的真正瓶颈——不是智能，而是现实世界的反馈速度：

"编程被如此迅速采用的原因是：你可以写近乎无限的代码、测试、运行，而外部世界不需要做任何不同的事。但药物研发需要数年测试，销售需要来回谈判，合同需要对方签字。AI也许能给你一个精妙的喷气涡轮叶片设计——但它大概率还是会失败，因为这就是前沿领域的基础概率。唯一的验证方法是造出来，然后试图摧毁它。这才是学习的真正极限，而它不在乎你有多聪明。"
— @levie

🛠️ 工具前线：Claude、Codex与"可抛弃代码"时代

产品层面，AI工具的日常使用正在走向成熟。@_catwu 分享了她用Claude Cowork管理日历的提示词——要求每周会议少于20小时、自动去重冲突、参考历史记录判断哪些会议她会拒绝。这种精细化的个人工作流配置，正成为进阶用户的标配。

与此同时，Dan Shipper 报告了一个里程碑式的突破：

"它刚刚越过了某个门槛。过去一周，我们能够自动完成约70%的人工校对编辑工作——这是有史以来第一次，而我已经尝试了好几年了。"
— @danshipper

@zarazhangrui 则提出了一个正在悄然改变开发者心智模型的观念转变：代码正在变得"可抛弃"。一次性的设计沙盒、帮助理解逻辑的临时HTML页面、用完即丢的仪表盘——当生成成本趋近于零，"写完就扔"反而是最高效的工作方式。

OpenAI Codex的UX问题也引发了讨论。Peter Yang 指出，对于非技术用户而言，"在云端运行此对话"这样的措辞完全不知所云；而点击Codex Web链接后又被引导去下载App，则是典型的产品文案失误。

🔐 网络安全：衡量超级智能的最佳基准？

Guillermo Rauch 提出了一个颇具洞见的论断：网络安全，而非"一键生成某某App的克隆"，才是测试模型真实推理能力的黄金标准。

"发现、修补、逆向工程、漏洞利用——这些需要超越编程语言、运行时和框架的认知能力，要求模型具备真正的推理力和'边角思维'。能做到这一点的人类极少，更别说在日常软件编写中体现出来。看到Kimi K3在这里表现出色，对开源模型来说是个好兆头。"
— @rauchg

⚽ 番外：世界杯决赛让硅谷"破防"

今天科技圈的另一个共同话题，是西班牙在世界杯决赛中击败阿根廷。Amjad Masad 高呼"Vamos España"，Rauch 则以一篇感人的"双重效忠"推文收尾——感谢阿根廷的斗志，也向西班牙送上祝贺。Matt Turck 则对阿根廷的战术颇为不满，吐槽整场决赛竟然零射正。技术圈的人，看球也这么讲究数据。
